quick: Analgesia 325-650 mg q4h; antiplatelet 75-100 mg once daily
Take with food or full glass of water to reduce GI upset
Avoid in third trimester; low-dose use only as directed
Caution; avoid in significant renal impairment
GI bleeding signs, renal function, tinnitus (high dose)
summary: Aspirin is a salicylate NSAID that irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase. Low doses (75-100 mg daily) provide antiplatelet cardiovascular protection; higher doses (325-650 mg) treat pain, fever and inflammation. Major risks are GI bleeding and bleeding generally; it must not be used in children/teens with viral illness due to Reye syndrome and should be avoided in the third trimester of pregnancy.
indications: Temporary relief of minor aches, pains and fever
Anti-inflammatory treatment of arthritis and rheumatic conditions (higher doses)
Secondary prevention of cardiovascular events (MI, ischemic stroke, TIA)
Acute coronary syndrome / suspected acute MI (loading dose)
Antiplatelet therapy after stenting/revascularization (with or without other agents)

dosage.d: Up to 3-6 g/day in divided doses
dosage.n: Monitor for salicylism; target levels if used

admin: Take with a full glass of water and with or after food to reduce gastric irritation
Swallow enteric-coated/delayed-release tablets whole; do not crush (except chewable in acute MI)
For suspected acute MI, chew a non-enteric tablet for rapid effect
Do not give to children or teenagers with chickenpox or flu-like illness (Reye syndrome)
Discontinue 7-10 days before elective surgery if bleeding risk outweighs benefit (per clinician)
moa: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), blocking conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxane A2. Inhibition of platelet thromboxane A2 (which platelets cannot resynthesize) produces lasting antiplatelet effect; reduced prostaglandins account for analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory actions.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs (including aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease)
Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding
Children/teens with viral illness (Reye syndrome risk)

preg: Avoid analgesic doses, especially in the third trimester, due to risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure, oligohydramnios, and bleeding/labor complications. Low-dose aspirin may be used in pregnancy only under medical direction (e.g., preeclampsia prophylaxis).
lact: Salicylate is excreted in breast milk. Occasional low doses are generally considered compatible, but avoid regular or high doses; monitor the infant for drowsiness, rash or bleeding.
renal: Use with caution; NSAIDs can reduce renal perfusion and precipitate acute kidney injury, especially with volume depletion, diuretics, or pre-existing renal disease. Avoid in significant impairment.
hepatic: Use caution in hepatic impairment and cirrhosis due to increased bleeding risk and potential for hepatotoxicity at high salicylate levels.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs, heparin) - markedly increased bleeding risk
Other NSAIDs (ibuprofen) - increased GI/bleeding risk and ibuprofen can blunt aspirin's antiplatelet effect
moderate: ACE inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics - reduced antihypertensive effect and renal risk ('triple whammy')
minor: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors - salicylate toxicity risk
interactions.food: Take with food or water to reduce gastric irritation; alcohol increases bleeding.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; concurrent alcohol substantially increases risk of GI bleeding.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect uric acid, glucose, and platelet function tests; high doses alter thyroid function tests.

emergency: Severe stomach bleeding (faintness, hematemesis, black/bloody stool)

monitoring: Signs/symptoms of GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis, faintness)
Renal function, especially in elderly or on diuretics/ACE inhibitors
Tinnitus or hearing changes (early salicylism) at high/anti-inflammatory doses
Bleeding when combined with anticoagulants or other antiplatelets
Salicylate levels in chronic high-dose anti-inflammatory therapy
counsel: Take with a full glass of water and food to limit stomach upset
Report black/bloody stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, ringing in the ears or unusual bleeding
Do not give aspirin to children or teenagers with fever, flu or chickenpox
Avoid alcohol and other NSAIDs; tell your doctor you take aspirin before any surgery or dental work
If for heart protection, take it daily as prescribed and do not stop abruptly without advice
pk: Analgesia 30 min; antiplatelet effect within ~1 hour
Plasma peak ~1-2 hours (delayed with enteric coating)
Aspirin ~15-20 min; salicylate 2-3 h (dose-dependent, up to 30 h at high doses)
Antiplatelet effect lasts the platelet lifespan (~7-10 days)
Store at controlled room temperature; keep dry
pearls: Antiplatelet effect is irreversible and lasts ~7-10 days (platelet lifespan) despite short plasma half-life
Chew non-enteric aspirin in suspected acute MI for fastest effect
Never use in children/teens with viral illness (Reye syndrome)
Ibuprofen taken before aspirin can block its cardioprotective antiplatelet effect - separate dosing
High-dose salicylism presents with tinnitus, hyperventilation and mixed acid-base disturbance
missed: For scheduled (e.g., daily cardioprotective) dosing, take the missed dose when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose; do not double up. For as-needed pain dosing, take only when needed within dose limits.
overdose: Salicylate overdose causes tinnitus, hyperventilation, respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia, seizures and coma. Treat with activated charcoal, IV fluids, urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate to enhance excretion, glucose, and hemodialysis for severe toxicity (high levels, acidosis, CNS or renal involvement). Monitor salicylate levels and electrolytes.
